lead: Join two different metals at two points and heat one. A small voltage appears, tens of microvolts per degree, depending only on the difference of the two junction temperatures. That is a thermocouple: the workhorse of industrial temperature measurement. It needs no supply, is small, cheap and rugged, covers −200 °C to 1600 °C, but its output is small, curved, and meaningless unless the cold junction is known.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.4 for the comparison with RTDs and thermistors, and Unit 1 for the calibration chain and error analysis.

sections.h3: Seebeck, Peltier and Thomson: where the volts come from

blocks.text: A thermocouple is a closed loop of two dissimilar metals with two junctions. Heat one junction and current flows; break the loop and you measure an emf. Seebeck reported this in 1821. Two effects build that emf.
Thomson effect: carriers at the hot end of a wire diffuse toward the cold end, leaving charge behind, so a wire across a temperature gradient has an emf along it.
Peltier effect: at a junction the metals have different carrier densities, so an electron crossing must gain or lose energy; a small emf sits at the junction.

The junction emfs oppose each other in the loop, so only their difference survives. Both junctions at the same temperature give exactly 0 mV, whatever that temperature is. Hence the cold junction must be known.

blocks.where: E is the Seebeck emf in mV; S is the Seebeck coefficient of the pair in µV/°C; T_h and T_c are the hot and cold junction temperatures in °C. The line is straight only over a small span; over a wide span S changes, so standard tables are used.

sections.h3: The three laws that make thermocouples practical

blocks.text: Three laws turn a pair of junctions into an instrument.

items: Homogeneous circuit: a loop of one homogeneous metal, with its ends at different temperatures, gives no emf. A single wire cannot measure temperature. Useful half: the reading depends only on the two junction temperatures, not on the temperature profile along the wires, provided each wire is homogeneous.

Intermediate metals: insert a third metal anywhere, with both ends at the same temperature, and the emf is unchanged. Copper terminals, solder, plugs and the amplifier input are allowed if each added pair is isothermal.
Intermediate temperatures: E(T₁,T₃) = E(T₁,T₂) + E(T₂,T₃). This refers all tables to 0 °C and lets the instrument add the cold-junction emf.

blocks.where: E(T_h, T_c) is the meter reading in mV; E(T_c, 0 °C) is the table value at the cold-junction temperature; E(T_h, 0 °C) is the table value you look up to get T_h.

blocks.text: Read backwards: the meter's millivolts are a temperature difference, never an absolute temperature.
Types are fixed by alloy pair. Sensitivities below are averages over the useful range; the curve is slightly nonlinear, so readings come from tables referred to 0 °C.

items: Good: no supply, self-powered, small and fast, rugged, cheap, wide range; type E is the most sensitive of the common types.
Bad: output of tens of µV/°C, so 300 °C is about 12 mV and needs a low-drift amplifier; nonlinear; needs a cold-junction reference; drifts if the terminal block drifts.

blocks.text: The instrument must supply E(T_c, 0 °C) itself. Three methods do it.

items: Ice bath: hold the cold junction in stirred ice–water at 0 °C, so E(T_c, 0 °C) = 0 and the table gives T_h directly. Accurate, laboratory only.

Hardware compensation: a bridge in the terminal block, with a thermistor or copper resistor in one arm, generates a voltage that follows E(T_c, 0 °C) and adds it. The element must sit in the same isothermal block as the terminals.
Software compensation: a second sensor measures block temperature T_c, the microcontroller looks up E(T_c, 0 °C), adds it, and converts the total to T_h. Most modern meters work this way.

blocks.text: Extension and compensating leads: the cable from probe to instrument must be the same alloy pair (extension grade), or a cheaper pair with nearly the same emf near room temperature (compensating lead). Copper is not allowed: it moves the reference junction to the probe head or junction box, where the instrument's cold-junction sensor cannot see it.
Keep both terminals on one isothermal block, clamped together and shielded from radiated heat. A gradient across the block appears directly as an error.

figure.caption: The cold junction never disappears — it only moves into the terminal block. Its own sensor supplies E(30 °C, 0 °C) = 1.20 mV, which is added to the measured 11.00 mV before the table lookup.

spec.aria: A chain from the hot junction through the thermocouple wires to the cold junction on an isothermal block, then an amplifier, a stage that adds the cold-junction emf, and a display.

examples.question: A K-type thermocouple produces 11.00 mV while its cold junction sits in a terminal block at 30 °C. K-type tables give E(30 °C, 0 °C) = 1.20 mV. (a) Find the emf referred to 0 °C. (b) Find the hot-junction temperature. (c) Find the average Seebeck coefficient.
steps: The meter measures E(T_h, T_c) = 11.00 mV, the emf between the hot junction and the cold junction at 30 °C.
Law of intermediate temperatures: E(T_h, 0 °C) = 11.00 + 1.20 = 12.20 mV.
K-type table at 12.20 mV, cold junction 0 °C: T_h ≈ 300 °C.
S_avg = 12.20 mV / 300 °C = 40.7 µV/°C, close to the nominal 41 µV/°C of type K.
examples.answer: E referred to 0 °C = 12.20 mV; hot junction ≈ 300 °C; average sensitivity ≈ 40.7 µV/°C.
examples.check:
E_meas = 11.00   # mV, meter reading at cold junction 30 C
E_cj = 1.20      # mV, E(30 C, 0 C) from the K-type table
E_hot = E_meas + E_cj
print(round(E_hot, 2))
T_hot = 300.0    # C, K-type table at 12.20 mV
print(T_hot)
S = E_hot / T_hot * 1000   # uV per C
print(round(S, 2))

traps: Reading the meter's millivolts straight from the table as if the cold junction were at 0 °C. That under-reads by roughly the cold-junction temperature.
Subtracting E(T_c, 0 °C) instead of adding it. The correction always makes the emf larger than the reading.
Using copper wire to extend the thermocouple. It moves the reference junction to the probe head, where the instrument's cold-junction sensor does not measure.
Unit slip: S is in µV/°C while tables are in mV, so 41 µV/°C × 300 °C is 12.3 mV, not 12.3 V.

quiz.q: State the law of intermediate metals and give one use.
quiz.a: A third metal inserted anywhere in the loop, with both ends at the same temperature, adds no net emf. Copper terminals, solder and connectors are allowed if each added pair is isothermal.

quiz.q: Which standard thermocouple type is the most sensitive, and what is its approximate Seebeck coefficient?
Why does a thermocouple need a cold junction? Why not just read the emf?
quiz.a: The emf depends on the difference of the two junction temperatures. Two identical junctions give 0 mV. The cold-junction temperature must be measured or held fixed before the reading gives a hot-junction temperature.

quiz.q: Why must the extension lead be the same alloy pair (or a compensating alloy) and not ordinary copper cable?
quiz.a: Copper extension moves the reference junction. The two copper-alloy junctions sit together at the probe head or junction box at its temperature T_box, they cancel as a pair, and the loop now reads E(T_h, T_box). The instrument still compensates for E(T_c, 0 °C) at its own block, so an error of about E(T_box) − E(T_c) is left. Matched extension or compensating wire keeps the loop's reference at the instrument block, where the compensation is measured.

quiz.q: A J-type thermocouple (iron–constantan) reads 8.12 mV, its cold junction is at 25 °C, and E(25 °C, 0 °C) = 1.28 mV. The hot junction is at 175 °C. Find the emf referred to 0 °C and the average sensitivity.
quiz.a: E(175 °C, 0 °C) = 8.12 + 1.28 = 9.40 mV. S_avg = 9.40 mV / 175 °C = 9.40 × 10³ µV / 175 °C = 53.7 µV/°C, near the nominal 52 µV/°C of type J.

quiz.q: A K-type probe in a steady furnace shows a slowly falling reading all afternoon while the furnace does not change. The instrument's terminal block warms from 25 °C to 40 °C. Explain with numbers.
quiz.a: K-type tables give E(25 °C, 0 °C) = 1.00 mV and E(40 °C, 0 °C) = 1.61 mV. If the meter does not compensate, the emf it sees falls by about 0.61 mV, which is 0.61 mV / 41 µV/°C ≈ 15 °C of apparent drop. The display falls by about the rise in terminal temperature.

quiz.q: A technician's terminal block runs at 30 °C at one screw and 36 °C at the other. What error appears in a K-type circuit, and why?
quiz.a: The intermediate-metals law cancels the terminal junctions only when they are at the same temperature. Here they sit 6 °C apart, so an extra emf of about 41 µV/°C × 6 °C ≈ 0.25 mV appears, roughly 6 °C of error. Fix: one isothermal block, both screws clamped together, shielded from radiated heat.

beyond: Not for the exam. A thermoelectric generator uses the same Seebeck effect directly; the Peltier cooler is the same device run in reverse, and a generator module is a cooler module driven that way. Thin-film thermocouples are deposited on silicon and turbine blades. Standard reference functions for each type are published as polynomial coefficients, which is how a microcontroller turns millivolts into degrees. Search for thermocouple reference function, isothermal block design and thermopile energy harvesting.
